source.title: Causal Localization of the Refusal Direction in Audio Language Models

page_placements.theme: Decodability is not control: the best-separating layer or direction is not the causal refusal handle

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It fits harmful-minus-benign difference-in-means directions and applies rank-1 projection ablations, as in the original method, in audio language models and tests their effects. Its localization protocol ablates sites independently rather than applying one direction at every layer.
record.gate_note: The paper reports causal margin effects, behavioral refusal-to-harmful-answer flips, a benign-prompt addition test, transfer tests, and controls. Decodability results are measurements, not causal outcomes. Values used only to select layers or set thresholds, and cited results from other work, are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: It applies the original harmful-minus-benign difference-in-means direction with norm-preserving ablation and addition in a new setting: five audio language models. Results are first-token refusal margins plus HarmBench-scored harmful-answer flips. It ablates one layer per run rather than one direction at every layer, so it is a new-setting test rather than a strict T1 replication.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add three points: a direction fit on the text LM backbone alone transfers to the audio model. The authors read the direction as refusal-linked rather than harmfulness-specific, because harmful and benign prompts also differ in form. They recommend auditing models with interventions rather than probes alone.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful-minus-benign difference-in-means directions and norm-preserving projection ablations, but localizes by ablating one site per run rather than ablating a selected direction at every layer. The study uses audio inputs and a first-token logit-margin readout; it also tests projector subspaces, rescue, addition, and cross-modal transfer.
record.method_sensitivity: The L16 effect depends on the benign prompt set: it is −7.10 with templated benign prompts and −1.79 after refitting with natural XSTest benign prompts. Effects also vary by layer/site, model, and modality-transfer direction.

fits_no_version.finding: The harmful-vs-benign contrast is nearly perfectly decodable (AUROC ≥0.997) even at L08, where single-layer ablation barely moves the margin.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear decodability of the harmful/benign contrast does not establish causal dependence of refusal on that layer's direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Directions and subspaces at the audio-to-LM interface have near-zero ablation effects in all tested models, while zeroing Qwen's encoder output shifts the margin by −4.7.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In audio LMs, refusal-margin dependence on a rank-1 contrast direction sits in the inherited LM band, not at the audio interface.

record.problems: The main prompts are synthetic verbatim TTS readings, so transcription-mediated transfer remains possible; human-recorded speech is untested. Harmful and benign prompts differ in form, and changing the benign set substantially reduces the L16 effect. The main readout is a first-token logit proxy, not full-text behavior; behavioral evaluation uses one HarmBench classifier, and its results are from separate runs. AF3's direction is fit in sample. General capabilities are not assessed.
record.rows_left_out: Not separately recorded: the remaining dense layer-by-layer profile values described in §3.1 and shown in Fig. 1; the reported profile replication across three further TTS voices; and the mixed-evaluator sign-of-margin agreement checks in §4. These are omitted because they are additional profile, voice-replication, or proxy-agreement results rather than separately reported outcomes for the claim versions' refusal behavior.

untested.parts: Preservation of general capabilities. Ablating a single selected direction at every layer (only single-site ablation and a joint L08–L15 ablation with per-layer directions). Full-text refusal rates after adding the direction to benign inputs (only the margin is reported).
No jailbreak analysis or adversarial training.
No affine, cone or multi-direction analysis of LM refusal geometry.
Harmfulness and refusal are not measured separately. The authors only interpret the direction as refusal-linked rather than harmfulness-specific.
Transfer across languages, base-to-instruct, and transfer of one fitted direction across different models. Each model's direction is fit separately.

missing.what: Random-direction control for the Qwen harmful-answer flip: 0.00 versus 0.75 for the fitted direction.

record.verdict_notes: V4 is untested: R2 is an interface subspace and R16 is a multi-layer ablation, not a refusal-geometry analysis. The reader's V1 'challenges' label for interface nulls is dropped, because V1 makes no claim about interface sites. Cross-model replications (R30–R33) are separate per-model fits, not V6 transfer. AF3's R30 is fit in-sample and left out of the verdicts. AF3 and Voxtral fail the safety gate. All speech is synthetic TTS, so transcript-mediated reuse of the text feature is possible.

versions.untested_parts: It tests single-site, all-position ablations and addition using a first-token refusal margin; it does not test ablating one direction jointly at every layer, and it does not assess general capabilities.
No weight edit or abliteration is tested.
No jailbreak attack or training against ablation is tested.

The study tests layerwise directions, a joint multi-layer ablation, and a rank-16 projector subspace. It does not test affine or cone models of refusal geometry, or multiple directions within LM layers.
It does not separately measure harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
It tests transfer between a text-backbone direction and the audio model, plus results across audio-model variants. It does not test languages or base-to-instruct transfer.
No refusal-training intervention or comparison of training procedures is tested.
